title: IF GRACE FORGIVES EVERY SIN… WHY NOT JUST KEEP SINNING?
paragraphs: IF GRACE FORGIVES EVERY SIN… WHY NOT JUST KEEP SINNING?
The question almost sounds offensive. But if we are honest, some of us have quietly lived as though the answer were yes.
There is a dangerous sentence a Christian can learn to say without ever speaking it aloud.

You know that conversation should not be happening. You know that relationship is pulling you somewhere dark. You know what you keep watching when nobody is around. You know what you keep hiding from your spouse. You know about the bitterness you have carefully renamed “discernment.” You know about the pride you disguise as confidence. You know about the secret habit you delete from your history but cannot erase from your conscience.
And somewhere between temptation and surrender, a thought whispers:
You ask Jesus to forgive you.
and somehow the mercy that should have made you love Him more becomes the excuse you use to walk back toward the thing that wounded your relationship with Him.
If that sentence made you uncomfortable, keep reading.
Because nearly two thousand years ago, the apostle Paul anticipated exactly this question.
“Τί οὖν ἐροῦμεν; ἐπιμένωμεν τῇ ἁμαρτίᾳ, ἵνα ἡ χάρις πλεονάσῃ;”
Ti oun eroumen? Epimenōmen tē hamartia, hina hē charis pleonasē?
“What then shall we say? Shall we continue in sin so that grace may increase?”
The Greek is forceful. Paul is not cautiously suggesting that continuing in sin might be spiritually unhelpful.
Because grace was never given so that sin could become comfortable.
Grace was given because sinners needed to be rescued.
“οἵτινες ἀπεθάνομεν τῇ ἁμαρτίᾳ, πῶς ἔτι ζήσομεν ἐν αὐτῇ;”
“We who died to sin, how can we still live in it?”

That is Romans 6:1–2, and the Greek text preserves the force of Paul's argument: the Gospel does not merely change the punishment awaiting the sinner. Union with Christ changes the believer's relationship to sin itself. Romans 6 goes on to describe believers as united with Christ in His death and called to walk in “καινότητι ζωῆς” — kainotēti zōēs — “newness of life.”
And when Christ saves a sinner, He does not merely forgive the old life so that the old life can continue undisturbed.
He begins making the sinner new.
That distinction may expose something many Christians desperately need to confront:
There is a difference between falling into sin while fighting it and planning to remain in sin because you expect grace to cover it.
The Corinthian church had serious moral failures.
The Bible does not sanitize its heroes because Scripture is not ultimately the story of impressive human beings.
It is the story of a holy God rescuing desperately sinful people.
But grace never turns rebellion into righteousness.
Grace never looks at the chains around your wrists and says, “Stay there.”
That is why Paul says something astonishing later in Romans 6:
“Sin will not have dominion over you.”
“οὐ γάρ ἐστε ὑπὸ νόμον ἀλλὰ ὑπὸ χάριν.”
“You are not under law but under grace.”
Notice what Paul does not say.
“You are under grace, therefore sin does not matter.”
therefore sin is no longer your master.
Grace is not permission to remain chained.
Grace is the announcement that Jesus Christ has broken the chains.
And perhaps that is where this becomes painfully personal.
Some of us do not actually want freedom from certain sins.
We want freedom from the consequences.
We want Jesus to remove guilt without touching the idol.
but we secretly negotiate with the Lordship.
“But please don't enter the locked room.”
And Jesus loves us too deeply to participate in that arrangement.
The Gospel is not Christ standing outside your prison cell whispering, “I forgive you for being inside.”
The Gospel is Christ entering our death, bearing our sin, suffering the judgment we deserved, rising victorious from the grave, and calling us out of captivity into life with Him.
That is why the cross destroys both pride and presumption.
No. Your sin was so serious that the Son of God went to Calvary.
“Then sin doesn't matter because Jesus paid for it.”
Look again at what your sin cost.
There was a crown of thorns.
The spotless Lamb of God carrying what sinners could never carry themselves.
So when temptation whispers, “It doesn't matter; God will forgive you,” look toward Calvary.
Grace does not make sin smaller.
Grace shows us how unimaginably great God's love is toward sinners.
Maybe you failed ten minutes ago.
Maybe you are reading this with shame still sitting in your chest.
The answer is not to run away from Jesus until you become respectable enough to return.
Bring the hidden thing into His light.
First John 1:9 tells believers that when we confess our sins, God is faithful and just to forgive and cleanse us.
Repentance does not mean you somehow purchase forgiveness by feeling terrible enough.
Repentance is the turning of a heart that finally stops defending what Christ came to save us from.
And sometimes repentance sounds less impressive than we imagine.
That prayer may be spoken through tears.
It may be spoken by someone who has prayed something similar before.
But the question is not whether you have ever fallen twice.
When you fall, where are you running?
Are you running deeper into darkness?
Or are you running toward Christ?
Because there is a world of difference between struggling against sin and making peace with it.
A person drowning will thrash desperately for air.
A person living underwater has accepted another environment.

Paul eventually describes the outcome of liberation from sin as fruit leading toward holiness, with eternal life as its end. Then Romans 6 closes with one of Scripture's most devastating and beautiful contrasts:
But the sentence does not stop there.
“τὸ δὲ χάρισμα τοῦ θεοῦ ζωὴ αἰώνιος ἐν Χριστῷ Ἰησοῦ τῷ κυρίῳ ἡμῶν.”
“But the gift of God is eternal life in Christ Jesus our Lord.”
And the gift has a name.
Grace is not God pretending you never sinned.
Grace is God doing for sinners what sinners could never do for themselves through Jesus Christ.
Grace does not say, “Your rebellion doesn't matter.”
Grace says, “Your rebellion was deadly, but My Son went into death for you.”
You don't belong to that master anymore.
Maybe somebody reading this has been using grace as anesthesia.
You keep numbing conviction with theological vocabulary.
But none of those truths were given to help us protect the sin Christ calls us to surrender.
“We are all sinners” is not the end of the Gospel.
And He begins transforming those He saves.
You may have mornings when temptation feels louder than worship.
You may stumble so badly that you wonder whether you have ruined everything.
But do not confuse the presence of a battle with permission to surrender to the enemy.
Cut off access to what repeatedly drags you back.
Ask another mature believer for help.
Pray when you do not feel spiritual.
Run toward Christ when shame tells you to hide.
Because the devil loves two lies.
“It's too serious for Jesus to forgive.”
Both lies are designed to keep you from the cross.
Sin is more serious than you wanted to believe.
And Christ is more merciful than you dared to hope.
And that is why Jesus rewrites everything.
If this exposed something you have been hiding, you do not need to tell strangers every detail.
There is no trophy for pretending.
There is grace for coming into the light.
And somebody you know may desperately need this truth tonight.
Send it privately to the believer who stopped attending church because shame convinced them Jesus no longer wanted them.
Send it to the person who thinks grace means sin doesn't matter.
Send it to the person who thinks their sin means grace is no longer available.
Because temptation has an interesting way of making us forget tomorrow what conviction made painfully clear today.

Scripture gives us a beautiful framework for Christian generosity. Paul instructed believers to give deliberately rather than impulsively, and he wrote that each person should give what he has decided in his heart, “not reluctantly or under compulsion,” because God loves a cheerful giver. Christian generosity is therefore worship offered freely to God, not a payment used to purchase His favor.
It does not make God love you more.
Jesus already paid the price we could never pay.
Let your local-church giving, generosity toward people in need, and support of Gospel ministry be matters of faithful stewardship before God.
And even if you cannot financially support the ministry, you can still help tremendously.
Pray that every word points beyond a page, beyond a ministry, beyond a personality...
Because Gospel Warrior is not the Savior.
A devotional is not the Savior.
A church building is not the Savior.
Your good behavior is not the Savior.
And perhaps after everything you have just read, one question remains.
“If I am saved by grace, do I have to keep sinning?”
You will still need grace every day.
You will still need confession, repentance, Scripture, prayer, Christian community, correction, perseverance, and the mercy of God.
But sin does not have to remain your king.
And the same grace that meets you covered in the dirt is the grace that refuses to leave you comfortably lying there.
Come with the confession you promised yourself you would never have to make again.
There is mercy at His feet.
There is cleansing in His blood.
There is life in His resurrection.
There is freedom under His Lordship.
And there is a future beyond the chapter you thought ruined your entire story.
The sin you thought would become the final sentence may become the very place where the world sees what Jesus can rewrite.
